node.description: An Australian historian of settler colonialism, race and the history of anthropology (1949–2016). His first book read Victorian and Australian anthropology through 'the elimination of native societies': 'the colonizers come to stay—invasion is a structure not an event' (1999). The 2006 essay made the formula a programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; after the frontier, elimination 'turned inwards' through allotment, blood quantum and assimilation, so the form stays 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims'. Race, he argued, 'is made in the targeting' (2001, 2006; Traces of History, 2016). Veracini called him the field's founder 'in a fit of absentmindedness'; Kauanui records that he 'insisted … that he did not create the field … that Native scholars did'. Critics find in his structure a 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch) and ask whether exploitation, not elimination, defines settler colonies (Englert).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016); “Nation and MiscegeNation” (Social Analysis 36, 1994); Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (1999); “Land, Labor, and Difference: Elementary Structures of Race” (AHR 2001); “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (JGR 2006); “Structure and Event” (in Moses, ed., 2008); “After the Frontier” (2011); “Purchase by Other Means” (2012); ed., “Recuperating Binarism” (2013); with David Lloyd, “Settler Colonial Logics and the Neoliberal Regime” (2015); Traces of History: Elementary Structures of Race (2016); ed., The Settler Complex (2016). Readers: Veracini (2011, 2016), Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014), Kauanui (2016), Goeman (2016), Birch (2016), the American Quarterly forum (2017), Englert (2020), Russell (2022).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md): the 2006 essay in full (an Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page; page numbers from Kauanui's citations), the 1999 introduction pp. 1–2 (earlier), Veracini's obituary, Goeman's memorial, Kauanui's essay, Macoun and Strakosch, Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel, Englert, in full or in most pages. Unread: the 1994 essay (JSTOR), the 1999 chapters (contents and catalogue checked), the 2001 AHR essay beyond a sentence he quotes himself, the 2008 chapter, the Settler Colonial Studies essays, Traces of History (British Library contents note only), The Settler Complex, Birch's obituary (restricted file), the 2017 forum, Russell's chapter. Life dates and places from Wikidata Q109284663 (checked by QLever SPARQL); posts from the Victoria University collection page (Victoria University, University of Melbourne, La Trobe University; undated) and Veracini's obituary (fellowships at Harvard and Stanford; undated), so no post is drawn as an event; Kauanui's 'English scholar' is noted against Wikidata's Australian historian born in Yorkshire. He did not coin the term (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, n. 7) and said he did not found the field; the entry presents a programme, not an origin. Canadian PhD figures are in the settler_colonialism scope_note, not here.

incident_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

incident_edges.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

incident_edges.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism set beside genocide studies: the Holocaust as 'the non-paradigmatic paradigm' against which 'qualified genocides' are devalued; 'structural genocide' proposed to retain settler colonialism's specificity without 'hierarchy among victims'; a chapter in Moses's Empire, Colony, Genocide (2006–08)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal"; "The best known of all genocides was internal to Europe"; Lemkin's definition (note 6); Hull, Pohl, Zimmerer and "the modernity of colonialism"; "the Holocaust, the non-paradigmatic paradigm that, being the indispensable example, can never merely exemplify"; "the term 'structural genocide' avoids the questions of degree—and, therefore, of hierarchy among victims" (p. 403 per Kauanui). The 2008 chapter in Moses ed. is unread (Berghahn contents; Docker's "Are Settler-Colonies Inherently Genocidal?" in the same volume). The holocaust entry is historiographical; this compares frames and does not claim he wrote Holocaust history. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Treaties, preemption, removal and allotment read as 'the logic of elimination' rather than as relations and encounter: 'the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute [the colonial state's] principal means of expansion' (2006); set against the fur-trade historiography's 'middle ground', which Veracini records as a rival recovery (2013)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), second section (the doctrine of discovery, preemption, the Cherokee removal: "The American right to buy always superseded the Indian right not to sell" (Rosenthal, quoted); "Rather than something separate from or running counter to the colonial state, the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute its principal means of expansion") and sixth section (allotment, blood quantum, termination). Veracini 2013, concluding section (author manuscript, read): "the recovery of a long lasting 'middle ground' between indigenous and settler polities in the past, sustained the possibility of renewed relationships"; "both the Canadian and US historiographies were late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis". edge_869 already compares the two fields; this names the person's own reading. Canadian material is not his. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Wolfe took from Harris the sentence that 'the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus' when capital's interest in uncluttered access to land is combined with settlers' interest in land as livelihood (2004, quoted 2006): a use as evidence, moderate
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), third section and note 36, quoting Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess?" (2004), p. 179: "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus." Englert 2020 (read) also uses Harris 2004, p. 172, against Wolfe. The direction matters for edge_1014, which found no derivation of Harris from Wolfe: the citation runs the other way. A single quotation; influence in the sense of a use as evidence, as for locB_rel_26 in revision 1.152. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Critiques address both Wolfe's model and its subsequent uses: Macoun and Strakosch question structural inevitability; Rowse questions a teleology of elimination; Englert directly challenges elimination as the defining logic. Kauanui defends Wolfe against formulaic citation while rejecting the replacement of Indigenous Studies (2013–20)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Macoun and Strakosch 2013 (author version, read): "SCT can depict colonization as structurally inevitable"; "Foundational scholar Patrick Wolfe has been labelled 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world'"; "a kind of colonial fatalism"; "it does not account for Indigenous lives". Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 (read): "treating settler colonialism as a meta-structure, thus erasing both its contingency and the dynamics that co-constitute" it. Rowse 2014 (abstract, existing): a "teleology of elimination". Kauanui 2016 (read in full): a criticism of Wolfe's reception rather than of Wolfe, defending the theory against the phrase that 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement' with it, and asking that "Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies". 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' is the citation graph's category for a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position (Sol review 1.156, finding 3). Englert 2020 (read in full): "a critique of the Wolfe-an model"; elimination "does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism, as claimed by Wolfe". Fairness: Kauanui and Goeman record his disclaimers and his engagement with NAIS; Macoun and Strakosch call his contribution "vital". (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Wolfe explicitly agrees that frontier closure marks a major change, interpreting the post-frontier shift through Indigenous containment and assimilation within continuing settler colonialism (2013).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary 257–259, especially 258, and 276 n 19. Qualified agreement is not blanket defense or proved influence. This remains an undirected comparison/reception link; Native sovereignty and continuing elimination remain central to Wolfe’s different account.

incident_edges.relationship: Wolfe uses O’Brien’s evidence on New England treaty status and earlier blood-quantum practices in his history of Indigenous racialization and dispossession.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own fresh selected2016body and actual endnotes: chapter5/n30uses Firsting203for disadvantages facing tribes dispossessed before US treaty relationships; chapter6/n92uses Firsting128for an earlier Connecticut blood-quantum example. These are two specific resources within one pair/kind, not evidence that O’Brien endorsed Wolfe’s entire comparative framework. O’Brien’s cited pages remain unread in full; Wolfe’s original legal/historical sources are not independently checked. Ebook PDF pagination is explicit and not passed off as print pages.

incident_edges.relationship: With Denise Henning (2021), Wheeler adopts Wolfe's definition: in the Americas 'classic colonialism evolved into settler colonialism', whose goal 'is the erasure of Indigenous peoples in order to establish settler rights to Indigenous lands and resources (Wolfe, 2006)'.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Henning and Wheeler, New Directions for Student Services 2020, nos. 171–172 (online 30 April 2021), section 'Colonization and intergenerational trauma' (early-view p. 3; print pp. 57–67); Wolfe 2006 (Journal of Genocide Research 8:4) in the references. A co-authored study (Henning first author) of rural Indigenous students' postsecondary experience: it uses the frame as historical context and does not discuss settler colonial studies as a field. Her earlier colonial analysis used Blauner's colonial model (1998) and postcolonial and anti-colonial theory (2000, 2010), without settler-colonial vocabulary.

named_group_routes.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the Settler colonialism entry. Greer argues the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others; commercial penetration, the fur-trade mode, is another. Most native–newcomer works predate the settler framework and do not adopt it. PhD context: among 2009–2026 PhDs engaging this roster (two or more people cited), the share also citing Wolfe’s or Veracini’s settler-colonial works rises from 1 of 66 (2009–14) to 14 of 88 (2015–19) and 26 of 65 (2020–26), while engagement with the roster holds steady (16.1% → 16.0% of all PhDs). Bibliographies record consultation, not adoption.

named_group_routes.relationship: Indigenous historical authority and settler-colonial analysis
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge settler colonial studies (abstract). Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_12) adds the read words on both sides. Kauanui 2016 (read in full): 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; Wolfe 'insisted … that Native scholars did' create the field; indigeneity 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'. Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, pp. 9–11 (read): the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study'. Goeman 2016 (read in full): Wolfe's work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies that at times leaves out Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies'. Veracini 2013 (author manuscript, read): 'indigenous studies, and especially history became crucial disciplinary sites in the development of "settler colonialism" as a conceptual category'. Comparison only: Indigenous history is not a subset of the paradigm, and the paradigm did not originate there. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note.

named_group_routes.relationship: Land, labour and elementary structures of race
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe's AHR forum essay and later book compare regimes of race through land and labour. Title level only: the weakest proposal, optional.

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler colonialism historicised as one mode of colonial invasion among several, beside imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism, dominant in some periods and regions of northern North America and not others: a sympathetic critique that keeps Wolfe's 'structure, not an event' (2018–19)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, all after 2000 and dated. 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (Journal of the CHA 30, 2019, read in full; a CHA keynote): settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians', but over 500 years of invasion 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the danger of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory' and, with Wolfe, settler colonialism is 'a structure, not an event'; 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); and 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' (p. 79). Property and Dispossession (2018), introduction read on Cambridge Core (no page markers): 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006). The target is the field, not patrick_wolfe: Greer accepts Wolfe's structure thesis and objects to how the term is commonly used, citing Woolford and Benvenuto's warning that it risks becoming 'a reductive shorthand' (p. 63). The William and Mary Quarterly essay (2019) is unread beyond its recorded opening.

named_group_routes.relationship: British Columbia's reserve system explained as geographical dispossession: a capacity resting on state-backed force, a momentum from capital and settlers, a legitimation in a discourse of civilization and savagery, and a management by 'disciplinary technologies' of maps, numbers, law and the land system (1997–2004); written in a settler society's terms ('successful settler colonialism', 2003), with no derivation from Wolfe's theory established by the texts checked, and faulted by reviewers for few Native voices
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words. 'Revisiting the Native Land Question', BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 137–151, his précis of Making Native Space, read in full: the reserves comprised 'slightly more than one-third of 1 per cent of provincial land' (p. 137); 'The capacity to dispossess rested on raw firepower authorized, usually, by the administrative superstructure of the state. … The momentum to dispossess came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods' (p. 137); 'The legitimation of dispossession lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery … the implementation of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies among which maps, numbers, and, especially, the common law were essential' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia. One is about progress and development … It rests, however, on the other basic story about this place, which is about dispossession, loss, marginalization, and the struggle for survival' (p. 140); 'Given the values and benefits associated with successful settler colonialism, many British Columbians will find this an exceedingly difficult commitment' (p. 144, of a politics of difference). The 2004 abstract (publisher's abstract via OpenAlex; article unread) states the same four conclusions: 'the initial ability to dispossess rested primarily on physical power and the supporting infrastructure of the state; the momentum to dispossess derived from the interest of capital in profit and of settlers in forging new livelihoods; the legitimation of and moral justification for dispossession lay in a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery …; and the management of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important.' In-period reception. Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia, BC Studies 117 (1998), pp. 64–67, read in full: Harris 'locates the non-Native settlement of British Columbia explicitly in the context of the expansion of European imperial and commercial power' and sees colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space that was formerly theirs into an immigrant society' (p. 64); but 'there are very few "Native voices" in it - something Harris himself admits', and Native peoples, 'despite a few examples to the contrary, emerge as victims' (p. 66); in the later chapters 'the connections to colonization … increasingly fade away' and class is not discussed (pp. 66–67); still 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67). Daniel Clayton, BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 5–11, read in full: 'Harris's most political work to date and arguably the most significant contribution to our understanding of colonialism in the province since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6). Jo-Anne Fiske, commentary in the 2003 forum (pp. 151–155, read): he 'says little … of how a change in mindset and a marshalling of political will might be achieved', and what he says of the symbolic 'is unsettling in its apparent simplicity' (p. 152); the powers he describes 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152). Harris replied: 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161). Val Napoleon (2004): see pe139_harris_rel_07. verification.note: Abstract read: the settler approach has much to offer, but across 500 years of invading Indigenous North America the settler variety dominates some periods and regions and fades in others. 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are other modes; extractivism has become predominant in recent decades. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry (Érudit PDF served to an ordinary request; text layer; folios 61–79, notes 80–86). Based on a keynote address to the CHA annual meeting (first-page note). Passages used: settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians' but 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the hazard of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality, as though the settler-colonial condition had no discernible beginning and as if it could never end' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory. I personally think it has a great deal to offer anyone trying to understand the present and the past of a country such as Canada' (p. 63); historians 'need to take on board the critique of settler-national historiography sketched out by Wolfe and developed more fully by others such as Lorenzo Veracini' (p. 63); 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'My objective is to try to historicize settler colonialism' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' as 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); settler colonization 'emerged as an important independent force' only from the last quarter of the eighteenth century (p. 70); 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' and 'An order based on territorial dispossession is not, and never has been, normal, natural, and inevitable' (p. 79). The source's page range 61–86 includes the notes. Addendum 2026-10-30: Fresh original Érudit 27-leaf PDF includes cover plus printed 61–86. Selected 61–64 and corresponding notes 80–81 reread; earlier complete 61–86 scope remains distinct. Greer values Wolfe and Veracini while extending the dyad, and explicitly proposes coexisting overlapping modes rather than chronological stages. Woolford/Benvenuto and Richter supply other critiques, not every one assigned to Wolfe. Named citation clusters and originals are not automatic personal formation. The article derives from a keynote; no full WMQ 2019 or original Wolfe reading is newly claimed.

incident_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

incident_edges.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

incident_edges.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." incident_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism set beside genocide studies: the Holocaust as 'the non-paradigmatic paradigm' against which 'qualified genocides' are devalued; 'structural genocide' proposed to retain settler colonialism's specificity without 'hierarchy among victims'; a chapter in Moses's Empire, Colony, Genocide (2006–08)

The 2008 chapter in Moses ed. is unread (Berghahn contents; Docker's "Are Settler-Colonies Inherently Genocidal?" in the same volume). incident_edges.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Greer adopts Wolfe’s critique of naturalized settler history and continuing dispossession while seeking a more differentiated colonial chronology.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2019:62–63 explicitly calls for taking on board Wolfe’s historiographical critique, developed further by Veracini, and values the structure-not-event formulation. Notes 2–3 and 7–8 distinguish Wolfe 2007,1999,2006 and Veracini 2010; originals remain unread here. Positive uptake coexists with Greer’s scope objection; neither automatic full agreement nor a direct personal teaching relationship is inferred.

incident_edges.relationship: Greer argues that Wolfe’s settlement–exploitation dyad needs extension to capture other overlapping colonial forms in northern North America.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2019:63–64 names Wolfe’s Australia/India focus, then introduces imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism as additional modes. Greer insists these coexist and overlap rather than form self-contained stages. He expressly values Wolfe’s critique and does not attribute every casual temporal flattening to Wolfe himself. Existing group critique edge_1012 remains; original Wolfe texts are unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the Settler colonialism entry. Greer argues the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others; commercial penetration, the fur-trade mode, is another. Most native–newcomer works predate the settler framework and do not adopt it. PhD context: among 2009–2026 PhDs engaging this roster (two or more people cited), the share also citing Wolfe’s or Veracini’s settler-colonial works rises from 1 of 66 (2009–14) to 14 of 88 (2015–19) and 26 of 65 (2020–26), while engagement with the roster holds steady (16.1% → 16.0% of all PhDs). Bibliographies record consultation, not adoption.

named_group_routes.relationship: Indigenous historical authority and settler-colonial analysis
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge settler colonial studies (abstract). Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_12) adds the read words on both sides. Kauanui 2016 (read in full): 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; Wolfe 'insisted … that Native scholars did' create the field; indigeneity 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'. Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, pp. 9–11 (read): the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study'. Goeman 2016 (read in full): Wolfe's work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies that at times leaves out Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies'. Veracini 2013 (author manuscript, read): 'indigenous studies, and especially history became crucial disciplinary sites in the development of "settler colonialism" as a conceptual category'. Comparison only: Indigenous history is not a subset of the paradigm, and the paradigm did not originate there. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note.

named_group_routes.relationship: Land, labour and elementary structures of race
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe's AHR forum essay and later book compare regimes of race through land and labour. Title level only: the weakest proposal, optional.

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler colonialism historicised as one mode of colonial invasion among several, beside imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism, dominant in some periods and regions of northern North America and not others: a sympathetic critique that keeps Wolfe's 'structure, not an event' (2018–19)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, all after 2000 and dated. 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (Journal of the CHA 30, 2019, read in full; a CHA keynote): settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians', but over 500 years of invasion 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the danger of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory' and, with Wolfe, settler colonialism is 'a structure, not an event'; 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); and 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' (p. 79). Property and Dispossession (2018), introduction read on Cambridge Core (no page markers): 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006). The target is the field, not patrick_wolfe: Greer accepts Wolfe's structure thesis and objects to how the term is commonly used, citing Woolford and Benvenuto's warning that it risks becoming 'a reductive shorthand' (p. 63). The William and Mary Quarterly essay (2019) is unread beyond its recorded opening.

named_group_routes.relationship: British Columbia's reserve system explained as geographical dispossession: a capacity resting on state-backed force, a momentum from capital and settlers, a legitimation in a discourse of civilization and savagery, and a management by 'disciplinary technologies' of maps, numbers, law and the land system (1997–2004); written in a settler society's terms ('successful settler colonialism', 2003), with no derivation from Wolfe's theory established by the texts checked, and faulted by reviewers for few Native voices
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words. 'Revisiting the Native Land Question', BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 137–151, his précis of Making Native Space, read in full: the reserves comprised 'slightly more than one-third of 1 per cent of provincial land' (p. 137); 'The capacity to dispossess rested on raw firepower authorized, usually, by the administrative superstructure of the state. … The momentum to dispossess came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods' (p. 137); 'The legitimation of dispossession lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery … the implementation of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies among which maps, numbers, and, especially, the common law were essential' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia. One is about progress and development … It rests, however, on the other basic story about this place, which is about dispossession, loss, marginalization, and the struggle for survival' (p. 140); 'Given the values and benefits associated with successful settler colonialism, many British Columbians will find this an exceedingly difficult commitment' (p. 144, of a politics of difference). The 2004 abstract (publisher's abstract via OpenAlex; article unread) states the same four conclusions: 'the initial ability to dispossess rested primarily on physical power and the supporting infrastructure of the state; the momentum to dispossess derived from the interest of capital in profit and of settlers in forging new livelihoods; the legitimation of and moral justification for dispossession lay in a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery …; and the management of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important.' In-period reception. Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia, BC Studies 117 (1998), pp. 64–67, read in full: Harris 'locates the non-Native settlement of British Columbia explicitly in the context of the expansion of European imperial and commercial power' and sees colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space that was formerly theirs into an immigrant society' (p. 64); but 'there are very few "Native voices" in it - something Harris himself admits', and Native peoples, 'despite a few examples to the contrary, emerge as victims' (p. 66); in the later chapters 'the connections to colonization … increasingly fade away' and class is not discussed (pp. 66–67); still 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67). Daniel Clayton, BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 5–11, read in full: 'Harris's most political work to date and arguably the most significant contribution to our understanding of colonialism in the province since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6). Jo-Anne Fiske, commentary in the 2003 forum (pp. 151–155, read): he 'says little … of how a change in mindset and a marshalling of political will might be achieved', and what he says of the symbolic 'is unsettling in its apparent simplicity' (p. 152); the powers he describes 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152). Harris replied: 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161). Val Napoleon (2004): see pe139_harris_rel_07. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: they cite Merivale, Kymlicka and Macklem, not Wolfe, and the books are unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Harris wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later reading, labelled: Perry (BC Studies 190, 2016, p. 112) says her 2001 book read British Columbia 'within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books'. A Bounded Land (2020), with its 'Postscript: The Boundaries of Settler Colonialism', is cited at title level only.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.

named_group_routes.relationship: Land as 'settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element': agriculture 'is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent' and 'progressively eats into Indigenous territory, a primitive accumulation that turns native flora and fauna into a dwindling resource' (Wolfe 2006); 'land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism' (Snelgrove et al. 2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), fourth section: "Of itself, however, modernity cannot explain the insatiable dynamic whereby settler colonialism always needs more land. The answer that springs most readily to mind is agriculture"; "Agriculture not only supports the other sectors. It is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent"; "The reproach of nomadism renders the native removable." Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, p. 30 (read): "land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism, and … environmental degradation has often proceeded through and in support of settler colonialism". Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 5 (read): "Within settler colonialism, the most important concern is land/water/air/subterranean earth". The dissertation evidence for the pairing is in the entry's scope_note, not here. Drawn by Agent B by the coordinator's decision; Agent C does not duplicate it. named_group_routes.relationship: Examines how British women’s struggles for prairie land combined gendered exclusion with unequal participation in Indigenous dispossession (Imperial Plots, 2016; read in corrected reprint 2018).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Read introduction pp. 3–11, 19–23. P. 6 explicitly engages Wolfe, while pp. 9–10 qualify settler women’s privileges and complicity; the later pages explain cross-border and imperial scales. The source now exceeds the prior publisher-page-only evidence, whose wording and date remain in its verification history. This contribution concerns this specific later work; it neither assigns her entire earlier bibliography to one paradigm nor asserts an influence relationship from the citation alone.

named_group_routes.relationship: Reads Kahnawà:ke membership disputes as carrying 'the punctuating, juridical bestowals of settler colonialism', with status designations inscribed on persons (2007); refusal as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society' (2017)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74; 2017 abstract (existing source, read). Nicoll (2015) quotes Mohawk Interruptus p. 3 on 'the structure of settlement that strangles their political form'. Wolfe appears in the 2007 article only as a supporting citation (n. 3); no critique of Wolfe is implied. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Defines colonial domination as power 'structured' to 'facilitate the dispossession of Indigenous peoples of their land and self-determining authority': 'Canada is no different than any other settler-colonial power' (2009); 'territorially acquisitive in perpetuity' (2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation p. 10, and p. 37: 'Canadian settler-colonialism remains structurally oriented around achieving the same colonial effect it sought in the pre-1969 period: the dispossession of Indigenous peoples of their lands and self-determining authority'; the 2014 book p. 125 as quoted by Englert (2020, read). Wolfe and Veracini are not cited anywhere in the dissertation (full-text search, 2026-10-28); for the settler-colony frame he cites Abele and Stasiulis, 'Canada as a “White Settler Colony”' (1989), at p. 18 n. 47; Englert's own critique of Wolfe is Englert's, not Coulthard's.
